Machine learning kinetics from molecular dynamics data

Jonathan Weare Email: weare@nyu.edu Affiliation: Courant Institute School of Mathematics, Computing, and Data Science,
New York University, New York, New York 10012, United States    Aaron R. Dinner Email: dinner@uchicago.edu Affiliation: Department of Chemistry and James Franck Institute, University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois 60637, United States
Abstract

Most molecular transitions occur on time scales far beyond direct molecular dynamics simulations. The committor, the probability that a configuration reaches a product state before a reactant state, is a central kinetic statistic, providing a mechanism-independent reaction coordinate and a foundation for transition path theory and the calculation of rates. This review surveys modern approaches for estimating the committor and related kinetic statistics from molecular simulations, with an emphasis on self-supervised methods that learn solutions of their defining dynamical equations rather than relying on labeled shooting data. We develop a common operator viewpoint connecting generator-based partial differential equations, variational principles, Markov state models, dynamical Galerkin approximation, and neural networks. Empirical and theoretical evidence points to the efficiency of these methods. We provide theoretical and practical guidance for realizing their full potential in applications, including strategies for treating non-Markovian effects and for sampling. We conclude by identifying opportunities for further research, including connections to reinforcement learning and generative modeling.

I Introduction

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are essential for connecting molecular structure to dynamics and function measured experimentally [1, 2]. Not only can simulations fully resolve microscopic dynamics, but energies and forces can be computed, and force field parameters can be varied systematically to probe their roles. This information can reveal mechanisms and guide molecular design. However, atomic-resolution simulations remain limited to time scales of ∼\sim10-5–10-4 s [3, 4], which prevents them from directly accessing the time scales of experiments and the phenomena that they probe (∼\sim10-3–104 s for the molecular examples that we describe in this review). This time scale gap makes observing one event in unbiased simulations prohibitively computationally costly, let alone the many needed for statistics and computing experimental observables.

In many cases, the time scale gap results from systems spending long times (many MD steps) in metastable states (reactants, products, and intermediates) interrupted by comparatively brief transitions between those states [5, 6, 7, 3]. This observation is the basis for almost all methods for enhanced sampling of events: simulations are biased toward key states with low probabilities either directly through progress variables or indirectly (e.g., by increasing temperature) and then the results are reweighted to recover unbiased statistics. While there are now well-established enhanced sampling methods for not only equilibrium averages [8, 9, 10] but also dynamical averages [11, 12, 13, 14], identifying suitable progress variables can be challenging for complex systems [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22].

This review discusses methods for computing statistics that can be used to identify suitable progress variables and to characterize states and pathways contributing to transitions. We focus particularly on the committor q⁡(𝐱)q({\bf x})—the probability that a trajectory starting from microscopic state 𝐱{\bf x} reaches the product state (BB) before the reactant state (AA) under the unbiased dynamics—and how it can be estimated efficiently from MD simulation data using machine learning methods. By definition q⁡(𝐱)=0q({\bf x})=0 for 𝐱∈A{\bf x}\in A and q⁡(𝐱)=1q({\bf x})=1 for 𝐱∈B{\bf x}\in B; q=1/2q=1/2 (equal likelihood of next reaching AA and BB) provides a definition of transition states that requires no a priori knowledge of a mechanism [23, 24, 15]. The committor is arguably the optimal reaction coordinate [23, 25, 26, 16, 27, 28, 29, 30, 22], and it is the central quantity in transition path theory for computing reaction rates [31, 32, 33, 34, 35], as we discuss below.

I.1 Rate theories

The traditional starting point of chemical reaction kinetics is transition state theory (TST) [36, 37, 5, 38, 39]. In TST, the rate constant kk is proportional to the equilibrium flux crossing a hypersurface that separates the reactant and product states. TST is exact when there are no hypersurface recrossings, but this is rarely the case for reactions in condensed phases, so TST generally overestimates rates. Kramers’ and subsequent theories improve on TST by accounting for the friction and curvature of the barrier [40, 41, 38, 39, 42, 43], but they still assume that the transition is dominated by a single, well-defined saddle point of the (free) energy. This assumption is violated in many systems studied today, ranging from surface-catalyzed reactions to protein conformational changes [44, 45, 46, 47]. These transitions can involve many competing pathways with broad and diffuse transition-state regions.

Transition path theory (TPT) [31, 32, 33, 34, 35] is a mechanism-agnostic framework for kinetics. TPT characterizes the statistics of the ensemble of reactive trajectories (or equivalently transition paths). The information about reactive trajectories is encoded in the stationary distribution, the (forward) committor, and the backward committor—the probability that, looking backward in time from 𝐱{\bf x}, the trajectory last came from AA rather than BB—all of which are functions of microscopic states, not paths. As we discuss below, for reversible dynamics, the unimolecular rate rA​Br_{AB}, the number of transitions from AA to BB per unit time, can be obtained by minimizing a variational expression for trial committor functions (see Section II.2). Note that rA​Br_{AB} is symmetric in AA and BB (rA​B=rB​Ar_{AB}=r_{BA}) and should be distinguished from the TPT rate kA​Bk_{AB}, which is obtained from rA​Br_{AB} by dividing by the proportion of time the process spends having last come from AA, i.e., by the stationary average value of the backward committor. Henceforth, “rate” in this review refers to rA​Br_{AB}.

For general dynamics (including dynamics that violate detailed balance), TPT computes the rate from an integral over a dividing hypersurface of the reactive flux expressed in terms of the stationary distribution and the forward and backward committors; in contrast to the rate theories described above, the dividing hypersurface is arbitrary, and the underlying trajectories may have any number of recrossings. The level sets of an approximate committor are natural choices in practice, and one can average over them to further suppress noise in rate estimates [48]. Some loss functions for training the committor covered in this review can also be used to estimate rA​Br_{AB} (see Sections II.2 and III.4). Ref. 30 connects TPT to Kramers’ theory.

I.2 Roadmap

TPT is a framework for computing reactive fluxes and rates given the stationary distribution and committors, but it does not provide a prescription for estimating these quantities from MD simulation data. As noted above, methods for computing the stationary distribution are well-established, at least in reversible systems [8, 9, 10] (see [14] for irreversible systems). We thus focus on the committor here.

Initially q⁡(𝐱)q({\bf x}) was computed by shooting: for a configuration 𝐱{\bf x}, one launches MM independent trajectories with momenta drawn from the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution and counts the number that reach BB before AA [23, 12, 28]. This approach is computationally costly because trajectories must be run all the way to AA or BB and accurate estimates require many trajectories for each 𝐱{\bf x} tested. Specifically, because the outcomes are binary (AA or BB), the error follows the formula for the Bernoulli distribution, q⁡(1−q)/M\sqrt{q(1-q)/M} [49, 28] (though the error can be reduced with empirical Bayes [50]). The error not only scales as 1/M1/\sqrt{M} but peaks at the transition state q=1/2q=1/2, which dominates rates and is of greatest mechanistic interest.

Ma and Dinner [15, 51] showed that one can regress on such data, which both combines information from multiple 𝐱{\bf x} and yields models of the committor in terms of candidate physical variables. Peters and Trout [52, 53] improved the data efficiency of this procedure through the introduction of aimless shooting, and they instead evaluated models with likelihood maximization. Jung et al. [21] made the sampling adaptive, alternating between training a model of the committor on shooting outcomes and selecting new shooting points that the current model places near the transition state. As we discuss in Section VI.1, these approaches have been used to learn the committor for a wide range of transitions. An advantage of methods that regress on small numbers of physical variables is that the resulting models are interpretable, but their accuracy is ultimately limited by the library of candidate physical variables. The requirement that the trajectories reach the reactant or product state can be hard to meet when systems have long-lived intermediates and/or highly diffusive dynamics.

These issues motivate approaches in which one represents the committor by a general parameterized functional form and then determines the values of the parameters so that the resulting function satisfies a defining equation of the committor. In the case that the dynamics are fully specified, the defining equation can take the form of a partial differential equation (PDE) [54, 55, 39]. For example, for overdamped Langevin dynamics, the committor is the stationary solution to the backward Kolmogorov equation (and the associated operator is the adjoint to the forward Kolmogorov/Fokker–Planck operator). When the PDE is high-dimensional, as is generally the case, it cannot be treated by traditional (e.g., grid-based) numerical approaches, whose computational costs scale exponentially with the number of variables. A successful alternative is to represent the committor by a neural network (NN), as we discuss in Section II.

However, when the analysis focuses on a reduced set of variables (e.g., by neglecting those of the solvent) for interpretability and/or statistical power, the partial differential form is not available, and the operator must instead be formulated as an expectation over the dynamics. The transition matrix in Markov state models [56, 57, 58, 59, 60], which is computed from statistics of state-to-state transitions within a lag time τ\tau in molecular dynamics simulations, can be viewed as an expansion of this operator in a basis of indicator functions. Dynamical Galerkin approximation and related methods [61, 48, 62, 63] generalize the expansion of the operator and committor to allow for other basis functions and to account for the boundary conditions q⁡(𝐱)=0q({\bf x})=0 for 𝐱∈A{\bf x}\in A and q⁡(𝐱)=1q({\bf x})=1 for 𝐱∈B{\bf x}\in B. These methods can achieve more accurate committors than MSMs, but they require choosing basis functions and the features on which they depend. NNs that learn functions that satisfy the operator equation and/or basis functions offer routes to going beyond manual feature engineering and are an active area of research [64], as we discuss in Section III.

To understand the distinctions between methods, it can be useful to categorize them from a machine learning perspective. The regression and likelihood maximization approaches described above are supervised in the sense that the tested configurations are paired with outcomes of independent MD simulations. The remaining approaches in this section can be considered self-supervised in that they test for satisfaction of equations and boundary conditions without requiring independent MD simulations; these approaches are the main focus of this review. Neural-network approaches that use fixed-point iteration to solve operator equations for finite lag times [64] are also closely related to temporal difference approaches in reinforcement learning [65].

In the remainder of this review, we introduce the mathematical framework for the self-supervised methods, which rest on the Markov approximation. Using this framework, we describe the methods more precisely and give examples of applications. We then discuss ways to go beyond the Markov approximation. We argue that good coverage in the transition region is important and discuss how it can be achieved through adaptive sampling. We end by briefly discussing alternative approaches and identifying areas that can be fruitful for further research.

II PDE approximation of the committor

Our starting point for computing the committor is its definition: q⁡(𝐱)q({\bf x}) is the probability that a system in state 𝐱{\bf x} reaches BB before AA. This probability can be obtained from the flux into BB from trajectories that start in 𝐱{\bf x}. An equation for this flux can be obtained from the backward Kolmogorov equation for the conditional probability p⁡(𝐲,t∣𝐱)p({\bf y},t\mid{\bf x}) [54, 39]:

∂∂t​p​(𝐲,t∣𝐱)=ℒ​p​(𝐲,t∣𝐱).\frac{\partial}{\partial t}p({\bf y},t\mid{\bf x})=\mathcal{L}p({\bf y},t\mid{\bf x}). (1)

In this equation, 𝐱{\bf x} acts as the argument to the function p⁡(𝐲,t∣𝐱)p({\bf y},t\mid{\bf x}), and the state 𝐲\bf y acts as a parameter. That is, the operator ℒ\mathcal{L} acts on functions of 𝐱{\bf x}, f⁡(𝐱)f({\bf x}).

The operator ℒ\mathcal{L} is the infinitesimal generator of the dynamics; it plays a role in stochastic dynamics that is analogous to the Liouville operator in classical mechanics (in fact, ℒ\mathcal{L} contains the Liouville operator when there is a deterministic component to the dynamics) [55, 66]. Specifically for an overdamped Langevin dynamics with force derived from a potential V⁡(𝐱)V({\bf x}), stationary probability π⁡(𝐱)∝e−β​V​(𝐱)\pi({\bf x})\propto e^{-\beta V({\bf x})}, position-dependent diffusion tensor D⁡(𝐱)D({\bf x}), and inverse temperature β\beta,

ℒf(𝐱)=eβ​V​(𝐱)∇⋅[e−β​V​(𝐱)D(𝐱)∇f(𝐱)].\mathcal{L}f({\bf x})=e^{\beta V({\bf x})}\,\nabla\cdot\Big[e^{-\beta V({\bf x})}\,D({\bf x})\,\nabla f({\bf x})\Big]. (2)

More generally, for the Markov process 𝐗t{\bf X}_{t} at time tt,

ℒ​f​(𝐱)=limτ→0+𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝐗τ)∣𝐗0=𝐱]−f⁡(𝐱)τ,\mathcal{L}f({\bf x})=\lim_{\tau\to 0^{+}}\frac{\mathbb{E}[f({\bf X}_{\tau})\mid{\bf X}_{0}={\bf x}]-f({\bf x})}{\tau}, (3)

where 𝔼\mathbb{E} denotes an expectation. Eq. (3) is essentially a definition of the time derivative, consistent with (1).

Integrating the flux equation, which has a form that parallels (1) with the flux replacing pp, gives [39, 67, 68, 69]

ℒ​q​(𝐱)=0for𝐱∉(A∪B),\mathcal{L}q({\bf x})=0\quad\text{for}\quad{\bf x}\notin(A\cup B), (4)

with q⁡(𝐱)=0q({\bf x})=0 for 𝐱∈A{\bf x}\in A and q⁡(𝐱)=1q({\bf x})=1 for 𝐱∈B{\bf x}\in B. Physically, (4) says that, an infinitesimal time later along each trajectory from 𝐱{\bf x}, the expected end state of the trajectory (AA or BB) is conserved.

Other kinetic statistics can be written in terms of equations of the generator as well. For example, the mean first passage time (MFPT) to BB from microscopic state 𝐱{\bf x} satisfies [55, 39]

ℒ​m​(𝐱)=−1for𝐱∉B\mathcal{L}m({\bf x})=-1\quad\text{for}\quad{\bf x}\notin B (5)

with m⁡(𝐱)=0m({\bf x})=0 for 𝐱∈B{\bf x}\in B. That is, an infinitesimal time later along each trajectory, the MFPT is one time unit less. More generally, this approach can be extended to conditional expectations of the form [55]

u⁡(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[Ψ⁡(𝐗σ)+∫0σR⁡(𝐗t)​𝑑t|𝐗0=𝐱],u({\bf x})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Psi({\bf X}_{\sigma})+\int_{0}^{\sigma}R({\bf X}_{t})\,dt\,\Big|\,{\bf X}_{0}={\bf x}\right], (6)

where σ=min⁡{t:𝐗t∈Ω}\sigma=\min\{t:{\bf X}_{t}\in\Omega\} is the time of first reaching Ω\Omega, and R⁡(𝐱)R({\bf x}) and Ψ⁡(𝐱)\Psi({\bf x}) are running and terminal “reward” functions. The committor corresponds to the specific choices Ω=A∪B\Omega=A\cup B, R⁡(𝐱)=0R({\bf x})=0, and Ψ⁡(𝐱)=1\Psi({\bf x})=1 for 𝐱∈B{\bf x}\in B and 00 elsewhere; the MFPT corresponds to Ω=B\Omega=B, R⁡(𝐱)=1R({\bf x})=1, and Ψ⁡(𝐱)=0\Psi({\bf x})=0, reflecting that no reward is collected upon reaching BB, but each unit of time spent before arrival contributes one unit to the total.

II.1 Physics-informed NNs (PINNs)

When an explicit form for ℒ\mathcal{L} such as (2) is available, (4) is a PDE. In this case, one can leverage methods for solving high-dimensional PDEs [70, 71, 72, 73, 74]. The general strategy is to represent trial solutions to PDEs by parameterized functions (qθq_{\theta} with parameters θ\theta for the committor) and to adjust the parameters to minimize the PDE residuals (ℒ​qθ\mathcal{L}q_{\theta} for the committor) [75, 76]. Software libraries now make NNs convenient choices for the parameterized functions (though others are possible [77, 78, 79, 80]). In the case of the committor, the part of the loss that enforces the PDE and thus makes the training physics-informed (PI) takes the form [81]

JPINN=𝔼𝐗0∼μ​[(ℒ​qθ​(𝐗0))2],J^{\mathrm{PINN}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\mu}\!\big[(\mathcal{L}q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0}))^{2}\big], (7)

where the subscript on the expectation indicates the distribution over which it is computed; here, μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}) is a user-chosen distribution with support on 𝐱∉(A∪B){\bf x}\notin(A\cup B). In practice, μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}) is represented by MM independent samples 𝐗0(1),…,𝐗0(M)∉(A∪B){\bf X}_{0}^{(1)},\ldots,{\bf X}_{0}^{(M)}\notin(A\cup B).

In addition, it is necessary to enforce the boundary conditions. A simple choice is to add to the loss above a term of the form [81, 82, 83, 62, 78]

JBC=𝔼𝐗0∼A​[(qθ​(𝐗0))2]+𝔼𝐗0∼B​[(1−qθ​(𝐗0))2].J^{\mathrm{BC}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim A}[(q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0}))^{2}]+\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim B}[(1-q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0}))^{2}]. (8)

The relative weights of JPINNJ^{\mathrm{PINN}} and JBCJ^{\mathrm{BC}} can be tuned by multiplying one term by a hyperparameter. Alternatively, one can use a construction that imposes the boundary conditions by masking the output of the neural network within the metastable states, e.g., qθ​(𝐱)=(1−χA​(𝐱))​[(1−χB​(𝐱))​q~θ​(𝐱)+χB​(𝐱)]q_{\theta}({\bf x})=(1-\chi_{A}({\bf x}))\,[(1-\chi_{B}({\bf x}))\,\tilde{q}_{\theta}({\bf x})+\chi_{B}({\bf x})], where the tilde indicates an intermediate output and χA\chi_{A} is an indicator function that equals 11 inside AA and 00 otherwise [84, 85]; in some cases [84], χA\chi_{A} is smoothed. With masking, qθ​(𝐱)q_{\theta}({\bf x}) satisfies the boundary conditions exactly for any θ\theta but can exhibit discontinuities at the boundaries of AA and BB; adding boundary penalty terms can mitigate these discontinuities [86, 87, 88].

The PINN loss is conceptually important, and it has the advantage that the distribution μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}) can be chosen freely. However, the second-order derivatives required (see (2)) can be problematic numerically: errors tend to be amplified, NN activations must be smooth, and the computational cost can scale quadratically with system dimension. For these reasons, researchers generally use other methods that we describe in the remainder of this review.

II.2 Dirichlet form

When the dynamics are microscopically reversible (i.e., satisfy detailed balance with respect to the stationary distribution π\pi), the generator is self-adjoint [55]:

𝔼𝐗0∼π​[f⁡(𝐗0)​ℒ​g​(𝐗0)]=𝔼𝐗0∼π​[g⁡(𝐗0)​ℒ​f​(𝐗0)]\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\pi}[f({\bf X}_{0})\,\mathcal{L}g({\bf X}_{0})]=\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\pi}[g({\bf X}_{0})\,\mathcal{L}f({\bf X}_{0})] (9)

for sufficiently smooth functions ff and gg. In this case, the committor can be obtained from a variational principle: among trial functions qθq_{\theta} satisfying qθ​(𝐱)=0q_{\theta}({\bf x})=0 for 𝐱∈A{\bf x}\in A and qθ​(𝐱)=1q_{\theta}({\bf x})=1 for 𝐱∈B{\bf x}\in B, the exact committor minimizes the Dirichlet form [55]

JDF​[qθ]=−𝔼𝐗0∼π​[qθ​(𝐗0)​ℒ​qθ​(𝐗0)].J^{\mathrm{DF}}[q_{\theta}]=-\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\pi}[q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})\,\mathcal{L}q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})]. (10)

Functionally differentiating (10) and integrating by parts shows that the minimizer satisfies (4).

Two further properties of the Dirichlet form hold regardless of whether the dynamics are reversible. First, evaluated at the exact committor, it equals the steady-state rate of transitions from AA to BB [33, 32]:

rA​B=−𝔼𝐗0∼π​[q⁡(𝐗0)​ℒ​q​(𝐗0)].r_{AB}=-\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\pi}[q({\bf X}_{0})\mathcal{L}q({\bf X}_{0})]. (11)

This result can be obtained by writing the rate in terms of the reactive flux through a dividing hypersurface. Second, for any generator of the form ℒ=a⋅∇+D:∇∇\mathcal{L}=a\cdot\nabla+D:\nabla\nabla with stationary distribution π\pi, where aa is the drift and ∇⁣∇\nabla\nabla is the matrix of second derivatives (e.g., (2)), the Dirichlet form can be rewritten as [55]

JDF[qθ]=𝔼𝐗0∼π[∇qθ(𝐗0)⊤D(𝐗0)∇qθ(𝐗0)].J^{\mathrm{DF}}[q_{\theta}]=\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\pi}\!\big[\nabla q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})^{\top}D({\bf X}_{0})\,\nabla q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})\big]. (12)

Combining these results with the variational principle, JDF​[qθ]≥JDF​[q]=rA​BJ^{\mathrm{DF}}[q_{\theta}]\geq J^{\mathrm{DF}}[q]=r_{AB} for reversible dynamics, so the Dirichlet form overestimates the rate for any qθ​(𝐱)≠q​(𝐱)q_{\theta}({\bf x})\neq q({\bf x}). This inequality can be interpreted as saying that the current associated with the exact committor, π(𝐱)D(𝐱)∇q(𝐱)\pi({\bf x})D({\bf x})\nabla q({\bf x}), carries reactive probability from AA to BB with minimum possible dissipation.

The form in (12) is widely used (typically with DD assumed to be position-independent, so it can be factored out of the expectation) [62, 84, 77, 83, 89, 78, 90, 91]. Applications include protein folding [92, 93], chemical reactions [92, 94], ion association/dissociation [95], crystal nucleation [96, 94], host-guest and protein-ligand binding [93, 95, 94], and membrane fusion [97]. Compared with the PINN loss (7), (12) requires only first-order derivatives of qθ​(𝐱)q_{\theta}({\bf x}) rather than second-order derivatives. However, because (12) ultimately derives from (9), it requires that data be drawn from (or reweighted to) the stationary distribution π⁡(𝐱)\pi({\bf x}). This requirement is statistically undesirable because it puts low weight on transition states, as we discuss further in Section V. Furthermore, minimizing the Dirichlet form to learn the committor is restricted to reversible dynamics; for nonequilibrium systems, the PINN loss or an appropriate trajectory-based method (Section III) must be used.

A practical limitation shared by (7), (10), and (12) is the requirement to evaluate the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} explicitly. When one wishes to model the committor as a function of a reduced set of variables 𝝃⁡(𝐱)∈ℝm\boldsymbol{\xi}({\bf x})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} with mm much small than the full dimension of the system (e.g., pairwise distances between selected atoms), the projected dynamics are governed by a generalized Langevin equation, which is non-Markovian: the dynamics of 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi} at time tt depend on its history, not just its instantaneous value. Even when the memory is sufficiently short that the dynamics can be approximated by an ordinary Langevin equation, the diffusion tensor D⁡(𝐱)D({\bf x}) is not directly available from the force field. Studies that apply (7), (10), or (12) to selected atoms implicitly assume DD is constant and isotropic, which is generally not the case. While various approaches for estimating D⁡(𝐱)D({\bf x}) from data exist [98, 99, 100, 101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106], they introduce statistical errors that propagate to the committor and the TPT statistics computed from it. This issue motivates the methods in the next section, which instead estimate kinetic statistics from trajectory data. Throughout the review we write the committor and other statistics as functions of the full microscopic state, q⁡(𝐱)q({\bf x}), even when the discussion concerns a reduced set of variables 𝝃⁡(𝐱)\boldsymbol{\xi}({\bf x}), to keep the notation uniform across sections.

III Learning the committor from trajectory data

There are many cases where it is not possible, or is undesirable, to evaluate the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} explicitly. These include not only the common case of analysis based on a reduced set of variables discussed above but also analysis of data from black-box simulators, experiments, and observations. In this section, we discuss approaches to compute the committor and other kinetic statistics from trajectory data saved at finite intervals τ\tau, without an explicit model for the dynamics.

III.1 Markov state models

Markov state models (MSMs) [56, 57, 58, 59, 60] are among the oldest and most widely used methods for approximating the long-time kinetics of molecular systems from trajectory data. One discretizes the space of dynamical variables into a finite number of states {Ω1,…,ΩN}\{\Omega_{1},\ldots,\Omega_{N}\} and estimates the transition probability matrix elements Ti​jτ=P⁡[𝐗τ∈Ωj∣𝐗0∈Ωi]T_{ij}^{\tau}=P[{\bf X}_{\tau}\in\Omega_{j}\mid{\bf X}_{0}\in\Omega_{i}] from the data. Statistics such as stationary distributions, relaxation time scales, and MFPTs can be computed from equations of the matrix 𝐓τ{\bf T}^{\tau}. In particular, the committor can be approximated by solving the linear system

∑j(Ti​jτ−δi​j)​qj=0for{i:Ωi∉A∪B},\sum_{j}(T_{ij}^{\tau}-\delta_{ij})\,q_{j}=0\quad\text{for}\quad\{i:\Omega_{i}\notin A\cup B\}, (13)

where δi​j\delta_{ij} is the Kronecker delta, and qi=0q_{i}=0 for Ωi∈A\Omega_{i}\in A and qi=1q_{i}=1 for Ωi∈B\Omega_{i}\in B. Applications of this approach include peptide folding [107, 108], dimerization [109], functional protein conformational changes [110, 111, 112], ice nucleation [113], and virus capsid assembly [114].

One can view 𝐓τ{\bf T}^{\tau} as the instantiation of the transition operator

𝒯τ​f​(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝐗τ)∣𝐗0=𝐱]{\cal T}^{\tau}f({\bf x})=\mathbb{E}[f({\bf X}_{\tau})\mid{\bf X}_{0}={\bf x}] (14)

in a basis of indicator functions on the states {Ω1,…,ΩN}\{\Omega_{1},\ldots,\Omega_{N}\} [17, 61]. From this perspective, (13) is the finite-τ\tau analog of (4) with the definition of ℒ\mathcal{L} in (3). As in the PINN approach above, an advantage of MSMs is that one has the freedom to choose the sample distribution μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}) because the statistics are conditioned on the initial state. In practice, the choice of μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}) affects the results in ways that depend on the choice of states and the approach used to estimate Ti​jτT_{ij}^{\tau} from finite data (both of which remain active areas of research) [115, 116, 117, 118, 59, 119, 120].

However, even in the limit of infinite data, MSM estimates for the committor have two sources of error. The first is discretization: every 𝐱{\bf x} within state Ωi\Omega_{i} is assigned committor value qiq_{i}. This source of error can be mitigated by using a fine discretization where the committor changes rapidly (i.e., the transition state region), which in practice, with finite data, spreads the data over more states. The second source of error holds even for an infinitely fine discretization: there is a τ\tau-dependent bias from the finite-τ\tau approximation of (4) [48, 121, 86]. In the next section, we address this finite-τ\tau error by introducing an operator that defines exact statistics; we then discuss various approaches for solving equations of this operator with expressive continuous representations, which address the discretization error.

III.2 The stopped transition operator

The finite-τ\tau error discussed above arises when trajectories that pass through the metastable states AA and BB contribute to Ti​jτT_{ij}^{\tau}. This issue can be addressed by defining an analog of (14) where the trajectories are stopped when they reach the metastable states [48]:

𝒮τ​f​(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝐗τ∧σ)∣𝐗0=𝐱],\mathcal{S}^{\tau}f({\bf x})=\mathbb{E}[f({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma})\mid{\bf X}_{0}={\bf x}], (15)

where σ=min⁡{t:𝐗t∈Ω}\sigma=\min\{t:{\bf X}_{t}\in\Omega\} is the time of first reaching a terminal state Ω\Omega and τ∧σ=min⁡{τ,σ}\tau\wedge\sigma=\min\{\tau,\sigma\}; for the committor Ω=A∪B\Omega=A\cup B.

The committor equation becomes [48]

𝒮τ​q​(𝐱)−q⁡(𝐱)=0for𝐱∉(A∪B),\mathcal{S}^{\tau}q({\bf x})-q({\bf x})=0\quad\text{for}\quad{\bf x}\notin(A\cup B), (16)

with q⁡(𝐱)=0q({\bf x})=0 for 𝐱∈A{\bf x}\in A and q⁡(𝐱)=1q({\bf x})=1 for 𝐱∈B{\bf x}\in B. The physical interpretation is the same as that discussed below (4), but now the time along each trajectory is finite (τ\tau or σ\sigma, whichever comes first). In analogy to equations of ℒ\mathcal{L}, equations of 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} can be written for other statistics of the form in (6) [48]. For example, the analog of the MFPT equation (5) is

𝒮τ​m​(𝐱)−m⁡(𝐱)=−𝔼⁡[τ∧σ∣𝐗0=𝐱]\mathcal{S}^{\tau}m({\bf x})-m({\bf x})=-\mathbb{E}[\tau\wedge\sigma\mid{\bf X}_{0}={\bf x}] (17)

with m⁡(𝐱)=0m({\bf x})=0 for 𝐱∈B{\bf x}\in B. In contrast to equations of 𝒯τ\mathcal{T}^{\tau}, which, as discussed above, are biased when trajectories are not stopped upon reaching terminal states, equations of 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} are exact for all finite τ\tau. This feature is important for taking τ\tau sufficiently long that the dynamics are effectively Markovian (as discussed further in Section IV). The methods that we now discuss solve equations of 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} using trajectory data without an explicit form for the operator.

III.3 Dynamical Galerkin approximation

Dynamical Galerkin approximation (DGA), which was first introduced in the context of equations of ℒ\mathcal{L} [61], solves equations of 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} such as (16) [48] by expanding statistics (here, the committor) in a basis:

qθ​(𝐱)=ϕ0​(𝐱)+∑ℓ=1Lcℓ​ϕℓ​(𝐱),q_{\theta}({\bf x})=\phi_{0}({\bf x})+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}c_{\ell}\,\phi_{\ell}({\bf x}), (18)

where ϕ0​(𝐱)\phi_{0}({\bf x}) accounts for the boundary conditions, and ϕℓ​(𝐱)=0\phi_{\ell}({\bf x})=0 for ℓ>0\ell>0 and 𝐱∈A∪B{\bf x}\in A\cup B; cℓc_{\ell} are coefficients. Substituting (18) into (16), multiplying by ϕk​(𝐱)\phi_{k}({\bf x}), and taking the expectation with respect to the sample distribution μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}) yields the linear system

𝐂τ​𝐜=𝐛τ,{\bf C}^{\tau}{\bf c}=\mathbf{b}^{\tau}, (19)

with

Ck​ℓτ\displaystyle C^{\tau}_{k\ell} =𝔼𝐗0∼μ​[ϕk​(𝐗0)​(ϕℓ​(𝐗τ∧σ)−ϕℓ​(𝐗0))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\mu}\big[\phi_{k}({\bf X}_{0})\,(\phi_{\ell}({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma})-\phi_{\ell}({\bf X}_{0}))\big] (20)
bkτ\displaystyle b_{k}^{\tau} =−𝔼𝐗0∼μ​[ϕk​(𝐗0)​(ϕ0​(𝐗τ∧σ)−ϕ0​(𝐗0))].\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\mu}[\phi_{k}({\bf X}_{0})\,(\phi_{0}({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma})-\phi_{0}({\bf X}_{0}))]. (21)

For other statistics of the form in (6), bkτb_{k}^{\tau} includes an additional term involving the running reward integral [48].

The entries of 𝐂τ{\bf C}^{\tau} and 𝐛τ\mathbf{b}^{\tau} can be estimated from a set of trajectory segments {(𝐗0(m),𝐗τ∧σ(m)(m))}m=1M\{({\bf X}_{0}^{(m)},{\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma^{(m)}}^{(m)})\}_{m=1}^{M}, where each segment starts at an initial condition 𝐗0(m){\bf X}_{0}^{(m)} drawn from a sample distribution μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}) and runs until time τ\tau or until reaching A∪BA\cup B, whichever comes first. As for the PINN loss and MSMs, μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}) can be user-chosen, and knowledge of its form is not needed; again, this enables freedom to concentrate the sampling where it is needed most. Once 𝐂τ{\bf C}^{\tau} and 𝐛τ\mathbf{b}^{\tau} are estimated, the coefficient vector c can be determined from (19), and the statistic can be computed from (18). In particular, given an approximate committor, the rate can be computed as an average over its level sets, as described in Section I.1 [48, 46], or using the estimators in Section III.4.

When the ϕℓ​(𝐱)\phi_{\ell}({\bf x}) are indicator functions for discrete sets of microscopic states, DGA reduces to MSMs built on the stopped rather than unstopped transition matrix; that is, the matrix is constructed to account for statistic-specific boundary conditions. However, other choices of basis functions can be made to avoid the discretization error discussed above. Strahan et al. [48] introduced a construction in which pairwise distances are multiplied by a function that vanishes on AA and BB; the resulting functions are then grouped into vectors and orthogonalized (whitened) through singular value decomposition (SVD). In related approaches, Khoo et al. [122] and Cao and Huang [63] consider polynomial, Fourier, and radial basis functions. Basis functions have also been learned: Thiede et al. [61] used diffusion maps, and Strahan et al. [64] used subspace iteration to train NNs. We discuss the latter in Section III.6.

III.3.1 Applications

Here, we showcase four simulation studies that illustrate how features of DGA enable accurate committor estimates and, in turn, mechanistic insight.

Trp-cage folding.

Trp-cage is a designed 20-residue fast-folding protein that has been studied extensively both experimentally and computationally (see Ref. 48 and references therein). Shaw and co-workers previously generated a 208 μ\mus trajectory [3], but it contains only 12–31 folding/unfolding events (depending on state definitions) [3, 123, 124] and thus little sampling of the transition state region. To address this limitation, Strahan et al. [48] generated a data set of short (30 ns) trajectories (totaling 30 μ\mus) distributed uniformly in selected pairs of variables, adding trajectories where replica-exchange umbrella sampling (REUS) revealed the unfolded state was undersampled. The resulting free energy, computed from an adjoint equation, agreed well with the REUS results, illustrating the advantage of accommodating an arbitrary sampling distribution. The committor was computed using the pairwise-distance basis functions described above and indicator functions on the pairwise distances and their time-lagged independent components. The pairwise-distance basis functions gave results that were the least sensitive to lag time, without the artifacts at the boundaries visible in the distance-indicator plots. Reactive fluxes projected onto selected variables allowed visualization of pathways and transition states (q≈0.5q\approx 0.5), which were consistent with earlier transition path sampling and shooting studies.

Insulin dimer dissociation.

The protein hormone insulin forms a homodimer that must dissociate to bind its receptor as a monomer. Beyond its importance for engineering analogs with tailored kinetics, this process serves as a paradigm for coupled (un)folding and (un)binding because the monomer is substantially disordered [125, 126]; the resulting dynamics are diffusive and multipathway, violating the assumptions of methods that require a well-defined transition state. Jeong et al. [46] seeded short (5 ns) unbiased trajectories from initial conditions drawn from previous umbrella sampling simulations [125], for an aggregate of just over 94 μ\mus, and used an indicator basis set on 45 features (i.e., a stopped MSM) to compute free energies, committors, and reactive fluxes (Fig. 1). They identified four dissociation pathways corresponding to rotations around three axes of the dimer structure and quantified, as functions of the committor, both the flux within each pathway and the exchange between them, which they rationalized in terms of the structure. Integrating the flux gave an inverse rate of approximately 100 ms, markedly slower than estimates from Kramers’ theory and its extensions [42]; the difference likely reflects the greater resolution of the DGA model, which does not project the barrier onto two dimensions. Characterizing a 100 ms transition with 94 μ\mus of data illustrates the power of DGA for studying rare events, i.e., ones that occur infrequently compared with thermal fluctuations.

Voltage sensing.

Voltage-sensing domains (VSDs), which underlie processes ranging from pain sensing to cardiac function, respond to changes in transmembrane potential by moving helices bearing positively charged residues. Crystal structures of a phosphatase VSD homologous to voltage-gated ion channel VSDs suggested a helical-screw mechanism in which the S4 helix translocates and rotates to exchange salt-bridge partners [127], but the details of the transition remained unknown. Guo et al. [47] analyzed 415 μ\mus of unbiased trajectories initiated from equilibrated REUS windows [128] and then extended adaptively toward conformations with q≈0.5q\approx 0.5 (Fig. 2). Because DGA enabled computing committor values for millions of sampled structures, the committor could be used as a reaction coordinate. The free energy as a function of the displacement charge was two-state, consistent with electrophysiological measurements, but as a function of the committor it revealed minima at q≈0.25q\approx 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75 (in addition to q≈0q\approx 0 and q≈1q\approx 1), indicating five-state microscopic dynamics. Sparse regression of the committor identified nine interpretable physical variables, which revealed a noncanonical helical-screw mechanism in which translation, rotation, and charged side-chain movements of the sensing helix are only loosely coupled. This mechanism explains why intermediates that give rise to complex kinetics in fluorescence measurements are hidden from electrophysiology measurements [129].

Hydrogen dynamics on catalytic surfaces.

In heterogeneous catalysis, many equivalent reactants and intermediates interact on a fluctuating surface, so the notion of a single well-defined transition state that underlies TST is generally inappropriate. McCandler et al. [44] analyzed association and dissociation of hydrogen on rhodium slabs and cuboctahedral nanoparticles, using an atomic cluster expansion machine-learned interatomic potential to generate 200 ns of trajectory data for each of four surface geometries at hydrogen coverages ranging from about 0.05 to 1.0 monolayer (Fig. 3). Rather than describing the system as a whole, they represented each hydrogen atom by 131 features of its local environment within 7 Å, reduced these to five time-lagged independent components, and clustered the result into states. Because the features are local in space, chemically similar environments at different locations on the surface are assigned to the same state, and the dynamics of the full system follow from aggregating over the individual hydrogen atoms. The committor for dissociation was computed by DGA with indicator functions (stopped MSMs), and the rate was obtained from the net reactive flux. The resulting rates agreed with TST in the dilute limit but deviated at higher coverage: trapping at corners and edges of the nanoparticles slowed association and dissociation, and hydrogen–hydrogen interactions caused the rates to depend nonmonotonically on coverage.

The results above show that DGA (including stopped MSMs) can yield accurate and informative results for systems of chemical interest. However, the expressiveness of these models is ultimately determined by the basis functions and the features that they take as inputs, and choosing them can be difficult for molecules and processes that are less well-characterized than the ones described here. NNs, which we introduced in the context of solving PDEs (Section II), address this issue by learning representations from data. The remainder of Section III focuses on NNs for learning the committor from trajectory data.

III.4 Variational methods for reversible dynamics

In the variational committor network (VCN) approach [85], one minimizes

JτVCN​(θ)=12​τ​𝔼𝐗0∼π​[(qθ​(𝐗τ)−qθ​(𝐗0))2]J^{\mathrm{VCN}}_{\tau}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2\tau}\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\pi}\!\big[(q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{\tau})-q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0}))^{2}\big] (22)

subject to the boundary conditions qθ​(𝐱)=0q_{\theta}({\bf x})=0 for 𝐱∈A{\bf x}\in A and qθ​(𝐱)=1q_{\theta}({\bf x})=1 for 𝐱∈B{\bf x}\in B. This variational principle, which can be derived by considering the TPT reactive flux through a dividing surface [130, 131], has been used with other function approximators as well [132, 133].

Eq. (22) reduces to the Dirichlet form (10) as τ→0\tau\to 0. To see this, note that stationarity of π⁡(𝐱)\pi({\bf x}) implies 𝔼π​[qθ2​(𝐗τ)]=𝔼π​[qθ2​(𝐗0)]\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[q_{\theta}^{2}({\bf X}_{\tau})]=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[q_{\theta}^{2}({\bf X}_{0})], so that expanding the square in (22) leaves

JτVCN​(θ)=−1τ​𝔼𝐗0∼π​[qθ​(𝐗0)​(qθ​(𝐗τ)−qθ​(𝐗0))].J^{\mathrm{VCN}}_{\tau}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{\tau}\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\pi}\!\big[q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})\big(q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{\tau})-q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})\big)\big]. (23)

Conditioning on 𝐗0{\bf X}_{0} and taking τ→0\tau\to 0, the factor τ−1​(𝔼⁡[qθ​(𝐗τ)∣𝐗0]−qθ​(𝐗0))\tau^{-1}(\mathbb{E}[q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{\tau})\mid{\bf X}_{0}]-q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})) becomes ℒ​qθ​(𝐗0)\mathcal{L}q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0}) by (3), and we recover JDF​[qθ]=−𝔼𝐗0∼π​[qθ​(𝐗0)​ℒ​qθ​(𝐗0)]J^{\mathrm{DF}}[q_{\theta}]=-\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\pi}[q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})\,\mathcal{L}q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})]. In this sense, (22) is the Dirichlet form with the generator replaced by a finite-difference approximation, allowing it to be evaluated from trajectory data without an explicit form for ℒ\mathcal{L}. Like (10), (23) should only be minimized to estimate the committor when the dynamics are reversible and the initial states are drawn from or reweighted to π⁡(𝐱)\pi({\bf x}).

When τ\tau is finite, trajectory segments can pass through the metastable states AA and BB or pass all the way from AA to BB or BB to AA. Because it is the finite-difference analog of (10), which applies only as τ→0\tau\to 0, (22) does not account for these possibilities: it uses the unstopped endpoint 𝐗τ{\bf X}_{\tau} rather than the stopped endpoint 𝐗τ∧σ{\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma}, which introduces a systematic error in the committor and rate estimates that grows with τ\tau.

Li et al. [82] introduced a related variational loss that does not suffer from the stopping issue. They split the average over trajectory segments into two contributions: segments that remain in the transition region for the full lag time, which propagate the trial committor qθq_{\theta} forward, and segments that reach AA or BB within τ\tau, which instead contribute the boundary values at the states they enter. However, the resulting parameter update is not the gradient of any loss function evaluated on finite data (though it is a consistent approximation of the gradient). Reducing the gradient to a single factor of ∇θqθ\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta} requires that the average of ∇θqθ​(𝐗0)​qθ​(𝐗τ)\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})\,q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{\tau}) over the data equal the average of qθ​(𝐗0)​∇θqθ​(𝐗τ)q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})\,\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{\tau}), i.e., that it not matter which end of a trajectory segment carries the derivative. Detailed balance guarantees that they are equal only for an average over infinitely many segments; for a finite data set, the two averages differ.

The exact variational committor network (EVCN) [86] addresses these issues. Each trajectory segment is divided into pieces at the successive frames at which it is in AA or BB, and the loss sums the squared change in qθq_{\theta} over the pieces:

JτEVCN​(θ)=12​τ​𝔼𝐗0∼π​[∑k≥0(qθ​(𝐗τ∧σk+1)−qθ​(𝐗τ∧σk))2],J^{\mathrm{EVCN}}_{\tau}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2\tau}\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\pi}\!\Bigg[\sum_{k\geq 0}\big(q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma_{k+1}})-q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma_{k}})\big)^{2}\Bigg], (24)

where σ0=0\sigma_{0}=0, σk+1\sigma_{k+1} is the first frame after σk\sigma_{k} at which the trajectory is in AA or BB, and qθ​(𝐱)q_{\theta}({\bf x}) is masked (Section II.1) so that qθ​(𝐱)=0q_{\theta}({\bf x})=0 for 𝐱∈A{\bf x}\in A and qθ​(𝐱)=1q_{\theta}({\bf x})=1 for 𝐱∈B{\bf x}\in B. For 𝐗0∉A∪B{\bf X}_{0}\notin A\cup B, σ1=σ\sigma_{1}=\sigma, the time of first reaching A∪BA\cup B used in (15); terms with σk≥τ\sigma_{k}\geq\tau vanish, so the sum is finite. Segments with σ>τ\sigma>\tau contribute only the VCN term in (22). In the remaining segments, the first and last pieces compare qθq_{\theta} at the start or end of the segment with the boundary value of the state reached first or visited last; these terms implement stopping. Each interior piece begins and ends in A∪BA\cup B, so it contributes 1 if it connects AA and BB and 0 otherwise. Together, the interior pieces count the complete transitions within the lag time; this count does not depend on θ\theta, but it makes the loss estimate the reactive flux itself, so that its value at the exact committor is rA​Br_{AB} for any τ\tau.

EVCN also symmetrizes the empirical loss by evaluating each trajectory segment together with its time reverse, so that the averages of ∇θqθ​(𝐗0)​qθ​(𝐗τ)\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})\,q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{\tau}) and qθ​(𝐗0)​∇θqθ​(𝐗τ)q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})\,\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{\tau}) are equal by construction rather than only in the limit of infinite data; the parameter update is then the exact gradient of the loss for any finite data set. Because of stopping and the transition count in (24), the EVCN loss can be used both to learn the committor for any τ\tau when the dynamics are reversible and to compute the rate from a committor estimate regardless of whether the dynamics are reversible. The value of τ\tau used to estimate the rate need not be the same as that used to estimate the committor.

Lorpaiboon et al. [86] compared VCN and EVCN loss functions for lag times spanning four orders of magnitude, using data for folding of Trp-cage and villin and for the left-right helix transition of a nine-residue peptide of 2-aminoisobutyric acid (AIB9). The two loss functions perform comparably at the shortest lag times, as expected because the VCN loss is exact for a single time step. Chen et al. [85] suggest choosing the smallest lag time that renders the dynamics effectively Markovian in the input variables, but care is needed. As τ\tau increases, the VCN committor flattens in the transition region until its predictions collapse to nearly a single value, and the corresponding rates fall off as 1/τ1/\tau (Fig. 4). EVCN committors remain accurate at all lag times tested, and their rates plateau near the empirical values computed from the trajectories. These results illustrate the practical importance of stopping trajectories when they reach AA or BB.

III.5 Minimizing the fixed-point residual

With stopping, the variational methods described in Section III.4 can yield highly accurate results, as compared with empirical estimates. However, as already mentioned, they require the initial conditions to be drawn from or reweighted to the stationary distribution π⁡(𝐱)\pi({\bf x}). Generally π⁡(𝐱)\pi({\bf x}) is large near the metastable states and small near the transition states, which are of greatest interest for learning mechanisms. Statistically, methods that allow for an arbitrary sample distribution μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}), as the PINN approach and MSMs/DGA do, enable concentrating sampling near the transition states and, more generally, adaptively sampling (as in DGA examples [48, 47] above). Here we discuss approaches that can learn the committor and other statistics of the form in (6) from trajectory data without an explicit form for ℒ\mathcal{L} or 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} and without assuming reversibility or π⁡(𝐱)\pi({\bf x})-distributed initial conditions.

III.5.1 The two-trajectory trick

The direct finite-τ\tau analog of the PINN approach is to minimize the squared residual of (16),

JFP=𝔼𝐗0∼μ​[(𝒮τ​qθ​(𝐗0)−qθ​(𝐗0))2],J^{\mathrm{FP}}=\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\mu}\!\big[(\mathcal{S}^{\tau}q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0})-q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0}))^{2}\big], (25)

with boundary conditions treated as described in Section II.1. One way to minimize (25) is to follow its gradient:

∇θJFP=2𝔼𝐗0∼μ[𝒮τ​qθ​𝒮τ​∇θqθ−𝒮τ​qθ​∇θqθ−qθ𝒮τ∇θqθ+qθ∇θqθ],\begin{split}\nabla_{\theta}J^{\mathrm{FP}}=2\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\mu}\big[&\mathcal{S}^{\tau}q_{\theta}\,\mathcal{S}^{\tau}\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}-\mathcal{S}^{\tau}q_{\theta}\,\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}\\ &-q_{\theta}\,\mathcal{S}^{\tau}\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}+q_{\theta}\,\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}\big],\end{split} (26)

where we suppress the argument of qθ​(𝐗0)q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0}) for clarity and use ∇θ𝒮τ​qθ=𝒮τ​∇θqθ\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{S}^{\tau}q_{\theta}=\mathcal{S}^{\tau}\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta} because 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} is linear. Each factor of 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} in (26) corresponds to an expectation conditioned on 𝐗0{\bf X}_{0} (see (15)). Because each of the last three terms on the right-hand side of (26) contains at most one such expectation, they can be estimated from trajectory data by means analogous to (20). By contrast, because the first term involves a product of two expectations conditioned on the same 𝐗0{\bf X}_{0}, it cannot be estimated consistently from one trajectory per initial condition; in general, for functions ff and gg

𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝐗τ∧σ)∣𝐗0]​𝔼​[g⁡(𝐗τ∧σ)∣𝐗0]≠𝔼⁡[f⁡(𝐗τ∧σ)​g​(𝐗τ∧σ)∣𝐗0].\mathbb{E}[f({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma})\mid{\bf X}_{0}]\,\mathbb{E}[g({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma})\mid{\bf X}_{0}]\neq\\ \mathbb{E}[f({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma})g({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma})\mid{\bf X}_{0}]. (27)

The two-trajectory trick resolves this issue by generating two independent trajectories from each 𝐗0(m){\bf X}_{0}^{(m)}, with endpoints 𝐗τ∧σ(m,1)(m,1){\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma^{(m,1)}}^{(m,1)} and 𝐗τ∧σ(m,2)(m,2){\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma^{(m,2)}}^{(m,2)}, and computing 𝔼𝐗0∼μ​[𝒮τ​qθ​𝒮τ​∇θqθ]\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\mu}[\mathcal{S}^{\tau}q_{\theta}\,\mathcal{S}^{\tau}\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}] as [81, 134, 135]

𝔼𝐗0∼μ​[qθ​(𝐗τ∧σ(m,1)(m,1))​∇θqθ​(𝐗τ∧σ(m,2)(m,2))].\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\mu}[q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma^{(m,1)}}^{(m,1)})\,\nabla_{\theta}q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma^{(m,2)}}^{(m,2)})]. (28)

Generating more than two endpoints per initial condition and averaging over distinct pairs can reduce the variance [81]. The two-trajectory trick thus enables computing the gradient in (26) at the expense of requiring multiple trajectories for each initial condition. Most available molecular dynamics data sets contain only one trajectory from each initial condition.

III.5.2 Fixed-point iteration

An alternative way to solve (16) that avoids the problematic term in (26) is the iteration [64]

qθk+1​(𝐱)\displaystyle q_{\theta_{k+1}}({\bf x}) =qθk​(𝐱)+η⁡(𝒮τ​qθk​(𝐱)−qθk​(𝐱)),\displaystyle=q_{\theta_{k}}({\bf x})+\eta\,(\mathcal{S}^{\tau}q_{\theta_{k}}({\bf x})-q_{\theta_{k}}({\bf x})), (29)

where qθk​(𝐱)q_{\theta_{k}}({\bf x}) is the model for the committor with parameters θk\theta_{k} at iteration kk. The hyperparameter η\eta controls the rate at which the model changes; η∈(0,1]\eta\in(0,1] guarantees convergence of the exact iteration (29). However, because qθk​(𝐱)q_{\theta_{k}}({\bf x}) is a parameterized function (e.g., an NN), one cannot directly assign it values as (29) suggests. Instead, the parameters must be adjusted to make the model as close as possible to the right-hand side of (29). Denoting the latter by q~\tilde{q},

θk+1=arg​minθ⁡d⁡(q~,qθ),\theta_{k+1}=\operatorname{arg\,min}_{\theta}\,d(\tilde{q},\,q_{\theta}), (30)

where dd is a measure of dissimilarity, the choice of which is discussed below.

In practice, the target q~\tilde{q} is not available as an explicit function; instead, for each initial condition 𝐗0(m){\bf X}_{0}^{(m)}, one obtains a random sample q~(m)\tilde{q}^{(m)} of q~​(𝐗0(m))\tilde{q}({\bf X}_{0}^{(m)}):

q~(m)=(1−η)​qθk​(𝐗0(m))+η​qθk​(𝐗τ∧σ(m)(m)).\tilde{q}^{(m)}=(1-\eta)\,q_{\theta_{k}}({\bf X}_{0}^{(m)})+\eta\,q_{\theta_{k}}({\bf X}_{\tau\wedge\sigma^{(m)}}^{(m)}). (31)

Masking, which again can be combined with boundary penalty terms to mitigate discontinuities at the boundaries (Section II.1), prevents errors in AA and BB from propagating to the rest of the solution.

The samples {q~(m)}\{\tilde{q}^{(m)}\} are unbiased but noisy. When one takes advantage of the fact that (31) requires only one trajectory per initial condition, one cannot average the noise pointwise and must instead treat it through the choice of dd used for the regression in (30). If ∇θd​(q~,qθ)\nabla_{\theta}d(\tilde{q},q_{\theta}) is linear in q~\tilde{q}, the errors in the individual targets average to zero over the data distribution, and the samples {q~(m)}\{\tilde{q}^{(m)}\} give an unbiased estimate of the gradient. Two standard losses that satisfy this condition are least-squares and binary cross-entropy,

d(q~,qθ)=−𝔼𝐗0∼μ[\displaystyle d(\tilde{q},q_{\theta})=-\mathbb{E}_{{\bf X}_{0}\sim\mu}\!\big[ q~​(𝐗0)​ln⁡qθ​(𝐗0)\displaystyle\tilde{q}({\bf X}_{0})\ln q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0}) (32)
+(1−q~(𝐗0))ln(1−qθ(𝐗0))],\displaystyle+(1-\tilde{q}({\bf X}_{0}))\ln(1-q_{\theta}({\bf X}_{0}))\big],

but the latter is the natural choice for a probability such as the committor. When the output of the network is constrained to [0,1][0,1] by a sigmoid, the gradient of a least-squares loss vanishes as qθq_{\theta} approaches 00 and 11, whereas that of the binary cross-entropy does not. Ref. 64 uses this construction and terms (32) the softplus loss. More generally, the dd functions with the required linearity properties for ∇θd​(q~,qθ)\nabla_{\theta}d(\tilde{q},q_{\theta}) are called Bregman divergences [136]. This requirement can be relaxed if one generates a swarm of trajectories per initial condition 𝐗0(m){\bf X}_{0}^{(m)} and replaces q~(m)\tilde{q}^{(m)} by a sample average approximation of q~​(𝐗0(m))\tilde{q}({\bf X}_{0}^{(m)}) as in Ref. 137. However, any remaining variance in those estimates leads to a bias in the corresponding estimate of ∇θd​(q~,qθ)\nabla_{\theta}d(\tilde{q},q_{\theta}). When η\eta is small, (29) approximates an ordinary differential equation; changing variables in that equation offers further flexibility.

Fig. 5 shows committor estimates for the AIB9 left-right helix transition. Excellent agreement is obtained between estimates from fixed-point iteration with many short trajectories and empirical references from long trajectories.

III.6 Subspace acceleration

Just as the eigenvalues of the transition operator 𝒯τ\mathcal{T}^{\tau} give relaxation time scales [57, 58, 56], the eigenvalues of the stopped transition operator 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} control the rate of convergence of the neural-network methods discussed in Sections III.4 and III.5 [64]. Because the boundary conditions are enforced separately (e.g., by masking, Section II.1), the part of qθq_{\theta} that is adjusted during training vanishes on A∪BA\cup B, and the relevant space consists of functions with this property. On this space, 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} has no eigenvalue exactly equal to 1 because each application of 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} transfers probability to A∪BA\cup B. When the time to reach A∪BA\cup B is long, as often occurs for the molecular transitions considered here, the dominant eigenvalue λ0\lambda_{0} approaches 1, and convergence becomes slow.

In this case, convergence can be accelerated by an iteration that also learns the dominant pp-dimensional eigenspace [64], in the spirit of block power iteration. This procedure shifts control of the rate of convergence to the gap between λp−1\lambda_{p-1} and λp\lambda_{p}. Operationally, one initializes pp NNs {ϕθℓ}ℓ=1p\{\phi^{\ell}_{\theta}\}_{\ell=1}^{p} and trains them through a nested iteration, repeated until convergence. The inner loop corresponds to the procedure described in Section III.5.2, in which noisy targets in (31) are generated and NNs are trained on them. The outer loop executes the inner loop and then ensures that the resulting functions do not become rank deficient, e.g., by QR decomposition.

The trained networks {ϕθℓ}ℓ=1p\{\phi^{\ell}_{\theta}\}_{\ell=1}^{p}, together with the result of the fixed-point iteration described in Section III.5.2, can be used as a basis for DGA to compute kinetic statistics. For the AIB9 left-right helix transition, subspace acceleration with p=5p=5 converges to the correct MFPT orders of magnitude faster than the basic fixed-point iteration in Section III.5.2 across all values of τ\tau tested [64] (Fig. 5F).

IV Beyond the Markov Assumption

The methods described in Sections II–III assume that 𝐗t{\bf X}_{t} is Markovian, i.e., that the future state depends only on the current state. This is the case by construction at each step of an atomic-resolution molecular dynamics simulation, when all positions and velocities are available. However, we generally compute statistics in terms of a reduced set of variables 𝝃⁡(𝐗t)∈ℝm\boldsymbol{\xi}({\bf X}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, and the coupling of these variables to the orthogonal ones that are treated implicitly makes the projected process depend on the history, i.e., there is memory [66, 138, 139]. When the dynamics have a separation of time scales, one can in principle choose 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi} that relax slowly compared with the orthogonal variables, so that the memory decays quickly and can be neglected. However, not all systems have a clear separation of time scales, and, even when they do, finding variables that minimize the memory can be challenging [140]. Discretizing the state space in an MSM and expanding a statistic in a finite basis in DGA (18) are also projections that introduce memory, even when 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi} are well chosen.

One way to test whether the memory is significant is to vary the lag time τ\tau. In MSMs, the implied relaxation time scales tk(τ)=−τ/lnλk(τ)t_{k}(\tau)=-\tau/\ln\lambda_{k}(\tau), where λk\lambda_{k} are the eigenvalues of the transition matrix, should plateau once the memory decays [57, 58, 56]. Because (16) is valid for any τ>0\tau>0 when the dynamics are Markovian, the committor should be similarly independent of τ\tau; other statistics based on the stopped transition operator 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} should be as well. Extending τ\tau until the memory decays comes at the statistical cost of decreasing the number of independent trajectory segments obtainable from a given amount of data. For this reason, it can be useful to account explicitly for history.

IV.1 Mori–Zwanzig formalism

The standard approach for treating memory in chemical physics is the Mori–Zwanzig formalism [138, 66, 139]. Projecting functions of the full state onto functions of the reduced set of variables 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi} separates the dynamics exactly into three contributions: a Markovian term that depends only on the current values of 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi}, a memory term that integrates the history of 𝝃\boldsymbol{\xi} against a kernel, and a term that reflects the dynamics of the orthogonal variables. Building on quasi-MSMs [141, 142, 143], Lorpaiboon et al. [144] used Mori–Zwanzig decompositions to reduce the error that the basis projection introduces to DGA. They derived explicit expressions for the forward and backward committors, the MFPT, and the stationary distribution in terms of analogs of the matrices and vectors in (20) and (21), which can be estimated from trajectory data. Because these expressions determine the memory at each lag from the correlation matrices together with the memory at shorter lags, the kernel is obtained recursively from data without assuming a functional form. Here the decomposition takes the form of a discrete-time generalized master equation, in which the memory term is a sum over times spaced by a short lag ρ\rho within a window τ\tau, with τ/ρ\tau/\rho a positive integer; taking τ/ρ=1\tau/\rho=1 recovers standard DGA. The orthogonal-variable term is neglected, but each term in the memory sum applies the complementary projection again, which removes the dynamics that the basis represents; when the basis captures most of the slow dynamics, the neglected remainder is smaller than the one standard DGA neglects.

It is worth contrasting quasi-MSMs and DGA with memory with traditional Mori–Zwanzig analyses [66, 139]. In the latter, the projection is typically onto a low-dimensional space, so that it is hard to capture all the slow dynamics and, in turn, to determine a memory kernel that yields accurate statistics. Many studies assume a functional form for the kernel, typically exponential. Studies that use more flexible parameterizations indicate that no simple universal form exists [145, 146, 147, 148, 149, 150]. The approach above determines the kernel from the data without such an assumption. Because quasi-MSMs and DGA with memory project onto many states or basis functions, which are often functions of many variables, they can retain most of the slow dynamics. The memory then decays rapidly, and few terms suffice, with most of the correction coming from the first term beyond the Markov approximation.

For a two-dimensional triple-well potential and the left-right helix transition of AIB9, memory reduced the lag time needed to match reference MFPTs and stationary distributions by about an order of magnitude [144]. Jeong et al. [46] employed DGA with memory in the insulin dimer dissociation study discussed above and found τ/ρ=2\tau/\rho=2, a single term beyond the Markov approximation, to be sufficient. Strahan et al. [64] extended the Mori–Zwanzig approach [151, 141] to the subspace acceleration described above; there, they applied it after the basis was learned, but it may also be possible to speed convergence by incorporating memory at each (outer loop) iteration.

IV.2 Delay embedding

Delay embedding is an alternative way to account for memory that is widely used in nonlinear dynamics. One augments the state with a window of nn previous observations, 𝐗~t=(𝐗t,𝐗t−ρ,𝐗t−2​ρ,…,𝐗t−n​ρ)\tilde{{\bf X}}_{t}=({\bf X}_{t},{\bf X}_{t-\rho},{\bf X}_{t-2\rho},\ldots,{\bf X}_{t-n\rho}) where ρ\rho is again a short lag, and then applies any of the estimators of Section III unchanged. The motivation is Takens’ theorem [152, 153], which states that a sufficiently long window of observations generically reconstructs the underlying state; once the window spans the memory time, the augmented process is approximately Markovian. The cost is that the state grows to m⁡(n+1)m(n+1) components for 𝝃⁡(𝐗t)∈ℝm\boldsymbol{\xi}({\bf X}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, offsetting the advantages of working with a reduced set of variables. Thiede et al. [61] and Strahan et al. [48] used delay embedding to reduce the number of variables needed to describe Fip35 WW domain and Trp-cage folding, respectively, to a few physically motivated variables. Delay embedding and the Mori–Zwanzig approach thus address the memory differently: the former enlarges the state until the dynamics are approximately Markovian, while the latter leaves the state unchanged and corrects the estimator. It would be interesting to compare the two with regard to data requirements and robustness to hyperparameter choices for a suite of high-dimensional models.

IV.3 Augmented TPT

History can also be used to extend TPT to statistics that depend on a sequence of events. Traditional TPT applies to trajectories connecting AA and BB, and it computes statistics by factoring the selection of reactive trajectories into quantities that are local in time. This factorization fails for statistics that depend on a sequence of events, such as the reactive current for only those trajectories that pass through an intermediate. Lorpaiboon et al. [154] showed that such statistics become accessible by augmenting the state with a label 𝐘t{\bf Y}_{t} that records the sequence of events in a trajectory, generalizing earlier history-augmented approaches, in which states are labeled by the last metastable state visited [155, 156, 157, 158]. Provided the augmented process 𝐙t=(𝐗t,𝐘t){\bf Z}_{t}=({\bf X}_{t},{\bf Y}_{t}) is Markovian, TPT applies to it unchanged. Lorpaiboon et al. [154] used this framework to resolve the reactive density, reactive current, committor, and conditional MFPTs for individual steps of a reaction through an intermediate and for individual pathways in a multipathway reaction. The framework can also treat reactions that traditional TPT cannot, such as cycles in oscillators and excitable systems, in which the reactant and product states coincide. Whereas the treatments above use history to address the memory that projection introduces, here the process is already Markovian and history enlarges the class of problems that can be addressed. Because augmented TPT also casts statistics in terms of quantities local in time, the estimators of Section III extend to it.

V Choosing the sample distribution

The methods discussed in Sections II and III and their requirements are summarized in Table 1. Except for the variational methods in Sections II.2 and III.4, one is free to choose the distribution μ\mu of initial conditions. In this section, we consider this choice, which is arguably as important as the estimator [159].

V.1 Mathematical analysis

Existing error bounds for MSMs [160, 161, 162, 163, 164, 121] were generally obtained from classical perturbation theory and are controlled by global quantities, such as condition numbers or escape times that grow exponentially with the barrier height in metastable systems [165]. Moreover, kinetic statistics can range over orders of magnitude, making relative, rather than absolute, error the relevant metric. Existing bounds, therefore, do not address whether statistics such as the committor can be practically estimated to a given relative accuracy for metastable systems.

When addressing this question, it is useful to distinguish two sources of error. Statistical error results from estimating transition probabilities from finite data. Approximation error remains even with infinite data because the basis is finite. Recently, Cheng and Weare analyzed statistical error for stopped MSMs on finite state spaces [166]. They bound the relative asymptotic variance directly in terms of local connectivity properties of the dynamics, without explicit dependence on condition numbers or expected escape times.

In the case of the committor, the bound takes the form

limM→∞M​Var​(q^i)qi2≤∑j,k;k≠jSj​kτμj​(Qj​kτ)2,\lim_{M\to\infty}\frac{M\,{\rm Var}(\hat{q}_{i})}{q_{i}^{2}}\leq\sum_{j,k;\,k\neq j}\frac{S^{\tau}_{jk}}{\mu_{j}\,\big(Q^{\tau}_{jk}\big)^{2}}, (33)

where q^i\hat{q}_{i} is the stopped-MSM estimate of the committor at state ii obtained from MM trajectory segments, ii is any state outside A∪BA\cup B, jj runs over states outside A∪BA\cup B, kk runs over all states, and μj\mu_{j} is the probability of state jj in the distribution of initial conditions. In this finite-state-space setting, 𝒮τ\mathcal{S}^{\tau} becomes a matrix whose j​kjk entry, Sj​kτS^{\tau}_{jk}, is the probability that a trajectory launched from state jj is in state kk at time τ∧σ\tau\wedge\sigma. The quantity Qj​kτQ^{\tau}_{jk} in the denominator is the probability that a trajectory launched from jj, observed at intervals of τ\tau, reaches kk before returning to jj and before reaching any state in A∪BA\cup B other than kk. The ratio Sj​kτ/(Qj​kτ)2S_{jk}^{\tau}/(Q^{\tau}_{jk})^{2} thus compares the probability of a direct transition from jj to kk within one lag time with the probability that the trajectory finds its way from jj to kk by any route. Because a direct step is one such route, Qj​kτ≥Sj​kτQ^{\tau}_{jk}\geq S^{\tau}_{jk}, and greater indirect connectivity lowers the bound. Notably, (33) does not depend on the expected escape time, which can be long when transitions are rare compared with thermal fluctuations.

Three conditions make the sum in (33) small. (1) No μj\mu_{j} in the denominator is too small. (2) Transitions between neighboring states remain probable as the state space is refined, so that a graph retaining only transitions above a fixed probability threshold stays connected. (3) Transition probabilities decay at least as fast as a Gaussian function of the graph distance between states, so that long jumps within one lag time are strongly suppressed.

When trajectory data are simulated, condition 1 is under user control, and it has immediate implications for the choice of sampling distribution μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}). In particular, the common choice μ⁡(𝐱)∝π⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x})\propto\pi({\bf x}) leads to μj\mu_{j} that shrink exponentially with barrier height, which inflates the relative asymptotic variance; (33) instead suggests that one should choose μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}) to avoid assigning very small probabilities to dynamically important states. Conditions 2 and 3 describe locality of the dynamics, which, for small to intermediate τ\tau, is reasonable to assume for molecular transitions with diffusive barrier crossings, the focus of this review.

Under the conditions above, Cheng and Weare show that the relative asymptotic variance grows no faster than the cube of the number of states NN. One factor of NN arises because spreading initial conditions over more states leaves each with a smaller share of the data, and two arise from counting pairs of states in the sum. In the model that they consider, the barrier height grows in proportion to NN, because the landscape is scaled so that neighboring states differ by about kB​Tk_{B}T. The bound therefore grows as the cube of the barrier height in units of kB​Tk_{B}T and, because the committor decreases exponentially with that barrier, as the cube of ln⁡[1/q⁡(𝐱)]\ln[1/q({\bf x})].

The relative asymptotic variance sets the computational cost, because the number of trajectories needed for a given relative accuracy is proportional to it. For shooting at a single configuration, the Bernoulli variance q⁡(1−q)/Mq(1-q)/M from Section I.2 gives a relative asymptotic variance of [1−q⁡(𝐱)]/q⁡(𝐱)[1-q({\bf x})]/q({\bf x}), which grows exponentially with the barrier height. The cost of the stopped MSMs discussed here instead scales polynomially. The advantage in aggregate simulation time is larger still, because each shooting trajectory runs until reaching AA or BB.

The advantage also depends on the lag time. As τ\tau grows, a trajectory segment long enough to reach AA or BB ends there, so the direct step becomes the only route from jj to kk that contributes, Qj​kτQ^{\tau}_{jk} approaches Sj​kτS^{\tau}_{jk}, and the summand approaches 1/(μj​Sj​kτ)1/(\mu_{j}S^{\tau}_{jk}), which is large for rare transitions. The relative asymptotic variance behaves the same way, approaching that of shooting as τ→∞\tau\to\infty. In numerical tests, the relative asymptotic variance is smallest at an intermediate lag time. The lag-time dependence compounds the statistical cost of long lag times noted in Section IV, and it strengthens the case for correcting the estimator for memory rather than extending τ\tau until the dynamics appear Markovian.

V.2 Sampling strategies

A central result of the previous section is that the choice μ⁡(𝐱)∝π⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x})\propto\pi({\bf x}) is inefficient and that μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}) should instead cover the transition region well. Distributing initial points in the latter way generally requires some knowledge of variables that can describe the transition. This might appear to present a chicken-and-egg problem because the best such variables are those that correlate with the committor. However, sampling can be initiated using variables that are sufficient for separating AA and BB; they need not specify the full mechanism. The results can then be used to guide adaptive sampling.

When one has access to previous data for a system, one can draw initial points from them. For example, DGA studies draw initial points from earlier umbrella sampling [47, 46] and temperature replica exchange [167] simulations. If no such data are available, reasonable initial points can be obtained by repeatedly gently steering the system through the transition, e.g., with adiabatic bias molecular dynamics [168], as in Refs. 48, 45. If comparisons with earlier simulations indicate that the regions of configuration space that contribute to the reaction are not sampled adequately, additional initial points can be added [48, 47].

Methods that sample unbiased trajectories as a means of exploring the state space, such as adaptive search methods [169, 60, 170], the string method with swarms of trajectories [171], and steered transition path sampling [172], could alternatively be used to obtain not only initial points but also an initial sample of trajectories. Some studies bias and correct the dynamics [173, 174, 175, 176, 85, 87], but because the variance of the reweighting factor grows exponentially with τ\tau, care is needed when pursuing this strategy.

More systematic sampling can be achieved through splitting and trajectory stratification algorithms such as weighted ensemble [177, 11, 178], forward flux sampling [179, 13], transition interface sampling [180, 181], milestoning [182, 183, 184], and nonequilibrium umbrella sampling [185, 14, 186]. These algorithms divide a space of progress variables into regions and launch relatively short unbiased molecular dynamics simulations so as to converge estimates of rates computed directly from sampled fluxes. While it is possible to modify these algorithms to obtain point estimates of the committor [156, 158], the trajectory segments that they sample can be used with the estimators that we describe here to obtain models of any conditional average of the form in (6). Furthermore, estimates of the stationary distribution from an adjoint equation of 𝒯τ{\cal T}^{\tau} can be incorporated into the sampling to accelerate its convergence [187, 188].

Given that the committor reports directly on transition progress, it is natural to use its estimates to guide sampling. Parrinello and co-workers use an iterative procedure that alternates between training NNs with the Dirichlet form in (10) [92, 93, 95, 96], or a surrogate for it [94, 97], and sampling with the bias potential −(1/β)​ln⁡(|∇qθ​(𝐱)|2+ε)-(1/\beta)\ln(|\nabla q_{\theta}({\bf x})|^{2}+\varepsilon), where β\beta is the inverse temperature and ε\varepsilon is a regularization parameter. Related adaptive schemes based on committor-dependent potentials were developed by Lin and Ren [189]. Other approaches improve coverage of the transition region using active importance sampling with umbrella sampling [83], the finite-temperature string method [89], or a generative model [190]. Chipot, Roux, and co-workers use the committor estimated with VCN to refine path collective variables [88, 87, 191], building on the committor-consistent string method [192].

As previously discussed, both the Dirichlet and its finite-τ\tau analog, the (E)VCN loss, require reweighting to the stationary distribution, which may offset the advantages of adaptive sampling. By contrast, estimators that allow for an arbitrary sample distribution allow concentrating initial points in the transition state region (q≈0.5q\approx 0.5) or distributing them uniformly over qq values. This strategy was pursued in the context of DGA [47], the two-trajectory trick [81], and fixed-point iteration [137] (as well as models based on full trajectories [103, 193, 194]). Whether the stability and convenience of the Dirichlet form and (E)VCN losses outweigh sampling flexibility likely depends on system properties, such as the presence of multiple pathways and intermediates, and it would be worth quantitatively characterizing the convergence of competing adaptive sampling procedures for reversible transitions.

VI Alternative approaches

VI.1 Shooting-based methods

While this review argues in favor of self-supervised methods for learning the committor owing to the control they afford in sampling, supervised shooting-based methods are used extensively and are under active development [22]. In particular, the Artificial Intelligence for Molecular Mechanism Discovery (AIMMD) method [21] couples a neural network that learns the committor on the fly from the outcomes of two-way shooting moves [12] with an adaptive scheme that uses the current committor model to bias the selection of new shooting points toward the transition region. The network represents the logit of the committor, ln⁡[qθ​(𝐱)/(1−qθ​(𝐱))]\ln[q_{\theta}({\bf x})/(1-q_{\theta}({\bf x}))], and is trained by maximizing the likelihood of the shooting outcomes treated as Bernoulli trials, which is equivalent to minimizing the binary cross-entropy. The network input is generally a library of candidate physical variables, from which the most important are identified and used for symbolic regression [21], although graph neural networks, discussed in Section VII.2, were recently used to remove the need to choose such variables [195]. Recent variants combine committor learning with transition interface sampling [194, 196], rejection-free shooting-point sampling that is uniform in the logit committor [193], or generative modeling [197]. Approximate free energies and rates can also be recovered from the data by reweighting [198, 193].

Methods that regress the committor on shooting outcomes (including but not limited to AIMMD) have been applied to a wide range of systems, including molecular isomerization [15, 199, 200], polymer and protein folding [21, 193], ion association and dissociation [201, 202, 21, 203, 199], nucleation [204, 205, 206, 207, 21], ligand (un)binding [194, 196, 195], molecular recognition for DNA repair [51], and membrane-associated processes [21, 208, 209, 210]. It would be useful to compare supervised methods, trained on shooting outcomes, with self-supervised methods, trained on trajectory segments, in terms of the simulation cost needed to reach a given accuracy in the committor and the rate. Such comparisons should span transitions with low and high barriers, with single and multiple reaction channels, and with and without intermediates.

VI.2 Dynamics emulators

An alternative to estimating kinetic statistics directly is to learn a model of the dynamics. Although doing so remains challenging with traditional approaches [211, 212, 213, 139, 214], machine-learned dynamics emulators are now successfully used for short-term weather prediction [215, 216], and they are improving in the molecular sciences [217, 218, 219, 220, 221, 222, 223, 224]. Unlike machine-learned force fields, which approximate the forces used in numerical integration, emulators attempt to approximate evolution over a time interval τ\tau much longer than a single MD time step. Trained on the same short-trajectory data used by the methods in Section III, emulators learn parameterizations of transition probability densities corresponding to the transition operator 𝒯τ\mathcal{T}^{\tau}. They can then be applied recursively to generate trajectories longer than τ\tau. Related generative models learn distributions of entire trajectory segments conditioned on selected frames [225].

Because they aim to replicate, at lower cost and often for a reduced set of variables, a trajectory that is statistically the same as would be generated by MD simulations, emulators can become trapped in long-lived intermediates, and the trajectories required to estimate the committor and other kinetic statistics by direct shooting can be extremely long. Yet, they often do not maintain statistical accuracy over time scales required to sample rare events [221, 222]. Despite substantial investment, these issues persist even in the weather and climate setting [226, 227]. Addressing them will require good sampling near transition regions [221] (Sections V and VII.4) and treatment of memory effects (Section IV), for the reasons highlighted previously in this review.

VI.3 Committor and optimal control
