Estimates of the committor allow a special form of biased sampling in which every trajectory becomes reactive. Doob’s hh-transform [228] with qq as the harmonic function hh (see (4)) defines the bias drift

𝐟∗=2D(𝐱)∇lnq(𝐱)=2D(𝐱)∇q(𝐱)q⁡(𝐱).{\bf f}^{*}=2D({\bf x})\nabla\ln q({\bf x})=\frac{2D({\bf x})\nabla q({\bf x})}{q({\bf x})}. (34)

Adding (34) to the drift of the overdamped Langevin equation (e.g., −βD(𝐱)∇V(𝐱)-\beta D({\bf x})\nabla V({\bf x}) for a system governed by potential V⁡(𝐱)V({\bf x})) reproduces, exactly and without reweighting, the reactive trajectory distribution of the unbiased dynamics [229]. The bias drift is proportional to D(𝐱)∇q(𝐱)D({\bf x})\nabla q({\bf x}), divided by q⁡(𝐱)q({\bf x}) so that the correction grows large where q⁡(𝐱)q({\bf x}) is small and the transition is least likely. Given an accurate approximation of the committor, one can generate trajectories to compute other statistics such as the rate for transition from AA to BB [91, 230]. Beyond the need for an accurate committor estimate, a practical limitation of this approach is that the reactive trajectories can be long when the pathway involves intermediate basins. In such cases, errors can accumulate and shift the distribution of trajectories and, in turn, estimates of statistics [231].

Among all possible drifts that reliably drive the system from AA to BB, (34) is the one that minimizes the Boué–Dupuis variational expression (cost functional) [232, 233]

−ln⁡q⁡(𝐱)=min𝐟⁡𝔼⁡[14​∫0σ𝐟⊤​D−1​𝐟​𝑑t|𝐗0𝐟=𝐱],-\ln q({\bf x})=\min_{{\bf f}}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{\sigma}{\bf f}^{\top}D^{-1}\,{\bf f}\,dt\,\Big|\,{\bf X}_{0}^{\bf f}={\bf x}\right], (35)

where we suppress the arguments of 𝐟⁡(t,𝐗t𝐟){\bf f}(t,{\bf X}_{t}^{\bf f}) and D⁡(𝐗t𝐟)D({\bf X}_{t}^{\bf f}) for clarity, 𝐗t𝐟{\bf X}^{\bf f}_{t} is the biased process, and, as previously, σ\sigma is the time of first reaching A∪BA\cup B. Trajectories with 𝐗σ𝐟∉B{\bf X}^{\bf f}_{\sigma}\notin B are assigned infinite cost, so the minimization is effectively over vector functions 𝐟⁡(t,𝐱){\bf f}(t,{\bf x}) that cause the process to end in BB. Using Girsanov’s theorem and assuming the diffusion tensor is unchanged, one can show that the expectation on the right-hand side of (35) is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of the trajectory distribution of 𝐗𝐟{\bf X}^{\bf f} with respect to the trajectory distribution of 𝐗{\bf X}.

Expression (35) offers an alternative route to the committor: one can optimize a trial drift directly. Because of the chain rule of KL divergence, the excess cost of a trial drift 𝐟{\bf f} relative to the optimal drift 𝐟∗{\bf f}^{*} is the KL divergence between the trajectory distributions they generate. More generally, the cost of any driven dynamics relative to the unbiased dynamics is a dissipation in units of thermal energy, related to a bound on rate enhancement established by Kuznets-Speck and Limmer [234]. Hartmann and co-workers [235] and Du and co-workers [236] use the hitting-time control problem in (35) to estimate the committor or its associated optimal control; the latter use a self-consistency relation analogous to the fixed-point iteration of Section III.5.2. Related finite-time control approaches condition trajectories on being inside BB at a prescribed terminal time [237, 238, 90, 230]. Others optimize control forces directly for rare-event and path sampling [239, 240]. These approaches are closely related to Schrödinger bridges, importance sampling, and variational path sampling, the latter two of which are reviewed in Ref. 241.

VII Outlook

Over the past two decades, studies that compute the committor and other mechanistically informative kinetic statistics have progressed from estimates with large uncertainties for tens of microscopic states to estimates with small uncertainties for millions of states; this transition enables qualitatively new types of analyses as discussed in Section III.3.1. This progress reflects the theoretical and computational advances described above, together with continued growth in computational power. An important remaining task is for researchers to deploy and evaluate these methods on the diverse chemical systems that motivate their research. We noted a number of specific open problems along the way; here, we highlight a few additional areas that we expect to be particularly fruitful in the near term.

VII.1 Connecting to reinforcement learning

The stochastic optimal control methods discussed in Section VI.3 seek to learn bias forces that make all trajectories reactive. This goal is shared by reinforcement learning (RL), which seeks to learn policies that map states to actions in Markov decision processes so as to maximize expected cumulative rewards. The RL connection to the committor more generally can be made precise: the committor is the expected reward (value function) when the reward is 1 on BB and 0 otherwise (with no discounting). In the language of RL, DGA is temporal difference (TD) learning with linear function approximation [242, 243]. The two-trajectory trick is a form of double sampling, which was introduced in RL to address an analog of the gradient estimation difficulty discussed in Section III.5 [244].

The RL connection also raises a potential tension between statistical efficiency and numerical stability. As discussed in Section V.1, efficient estimation of transition statistics can require sampling initial conditions from a distribution μ⁡(𝐱)\mu({\bf x}) that differs substantially from the stationary distribution π⁡(𝐱)\pi({\bf x}). The fixed-point iteration in Section III.5.2 combines this freedom with function approximation and bootstrapping, since the current estimate qθk​(𝐱)q_{\theta_{k}}({\bf x}) is used to construct the target for qθk+1​(𝐱)q_{\theta_{k+1}}({\bf x}). This setting is closely related to the “deadly triad” in RL. When fixed-point iterations are projected, mismatch between the sampling distribution and the dynamics can invalidate standard contraction arguments for convergence guarantees, and worst-case examples can diverge [65, 245]. This does not imply that the fixed-point scheme is unstable in practice but suggests that sampling strategies chosen for statistical efficiency should also be examined for their effect on numerical stability. RL may provide useful tools for understanding and controlling this tradeoff.

VII.2 Reducing feature engineering

Existing NNs for the committor rely on manually selected features or on Cartesian coordinates aligned on manually selected atoms. Equivariant geometric graph NNs (GNNs), in which information is passed between graph nodes that correspond to atom positions, are promising alternatives because they can take Cartesian coordinates as inputs while respecting molecular symmetries. In principle, then, the analysis can proceed from atomic coordinates alone, and the features relevant to the dynamics can be learned rather than chosen in advance. GNNs were used to compute committors for a variety of peptide conformational transitions (including Trp-cage folding), chemical reactions (Diels–Alder), and associations/dissociations (NaCl, CaCO3, and host-guest and protein-ligand systems) [95, 246, 195]. GNNs were also used to learn state definitions [247, 248, 249], which can strongly affect estimates of kinetic statistics.

However, GNNs can be memory- and runtime-limited. This cost is compounded when avoiding data leakage requires splitting training and validation sets by trajectory rather than by time-lagged pair, because each trajectory-level split must then use a large minibatch to preserve sampling diversity [248, 249]. Two developments can extend the tractable number of nodes by orders of magnitude. One pre-trains a GNN on a tractable task and then fixes its parameters, optimizing only an output head specific to the dynamics analysis [248]; the other merges information across windows of residues without compromising model expressiveness [249]. How best to ensure stability when training such expressive models is an open question, as is how to interpret them.

VII.3 Interpretation

Presently the main route to interpreting the committor is to choose a library of candidate physical variables and fit a model that depends on a small number of those variables to either shooting data [15, 21, 210, 196, 200, 22] or a model of the committor obtained from the methods described in Sections II and III [47]. Correlations with the committor [46], gradient-based sensitivity analyses [194], and systematic approaches for identifying important features [199] such as Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) [250] and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) [251] are also used. Though reasonable, these approaches can only discover variables in the library, and human intuition is still needed to translate the identified variables into mechanisms. Methods that allow one to discover new features are an active area of research. Sparse autoencoders were recently used to learn features from trained models for protein structure and binding prediction [252, 253], and it would be interesting to apply them in the context of dynamics. The average gradient outer product (AGOP), used to explain how neural networks learn features [254], was recently applied to extract physically interpretable feature directions directly from a neural network trained to forecast ocean-atmosphere dynamics [255]. Closely related decompositions of rates and entropy production into contributions from specified coordinates already exist for stochastic dynamics [90, 256]; for Hamiltonian dynamics, Ma and co-workers decompose potential and kinetic energy flows and obtain coordinates from singular vectors of a generalization of these flows, the generalized work functional [257, 258, 259, 260, 22]. Using the eigenvectors of the AGOP for a model of the committor could offer a data-driven alternative to a predefined variable library, although the resulting directions would still require interpretation. Given advances in agentic hypothesis generation [261, 262, 263], we expect automated reasoning about candidate mechanisms to soon complement feature-importance and feature-discovery methods.

VII.4 Generative machine learning

The methods discussed in Sections II and III regress on data to estimate kinetic statistics. Generative machine learning methods instead learn distributions. They can be used to sample initial points [264, 265, 266, 197, 170] and, because successive points sampled are uncorrelated, they complement the MD-based approaches discussed in Section V.2, which must traverse distributions. However, nothing guarantees that a generative model’s learned distribution corresponds to a physically meaningful statistical ensemble, and such models can miss important states entirely [267, 268]. Reweighting the generated ensemble after the fact is ineffective when it overlaps little with the target, which is the same obstacle that makes equilibrium sampling inefficient for committor estimation (Section V).

Recent studies address these issues by coupling generative models with committor learning in self-consistent loops to concentrate sampling near q≈0.5q\approx 0.5, instead of training on an equilibrium (Boltzmann) ensemble [266, 197]; the Gen-COMPAS method [266], which combines diffusion models with VCN, is demonstrated on Trp-cage folding, coupled folding and ligand binding of ribose-binding protein, and conformational transitions in three membrane proteins (the mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier, the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, and a vacuolar ATPase), recovering a substrate-dependent transport mechanism and an asymmetric receptor-activation pathway subsequently corroborated by an independent experiment [269].

The examples immediately above leverage MD simulations for transition-path sampling, but in principle, generative models can also be used directly [270, 225, 271, 272]. However, models trained on Boltzmann-weighted configurations are unreliable near transition states because these regions are poorly represented in the training data. Approaches now being developed to address this problem follow two general strategies. The first is that, as espoused throughout this review, one should place data where accuracy is needed: training on restrained distributions concentrates samples in selected regions, and an appropriately conditioned noising process removes the resulting bias, so that the model recovers the unrestrained target without importance weights [273]. The second is that physical consistency can be enforced during inference rather than learned: alternating generative and MD updates in a Gibbs sampler composes a pretrained model for selected variables with explicit context for the rest, with conditions under which this is exact [274], in contrast to heuristic guidance terms. Because this construction requires only local conditionals, it extends to any path ensemble with Markov structure [275]. Outperforming MD is likely to require combining such strategies, particularly once the cost of generating training data is taken into account, and whether transferable models can offset this cost remains to be shown.

VIII Conclusions

In this review, we discussed methods for computing kinetic statistics that reveal microscopic mechanisms. A recurring theme was the advantage of estimating these statistics directly from trajectory data rather than from an assumed form for the dynamics; this approach extends naturally to systems for which the form of the dynamics is unknown, including reduced sets of variables, irreversible dynamics, and experimental time series. Key technical points were the importance of stopping trajectories at the boundaries of the metastable states and achieving good sampling in transition regions. We discussed how the committor can be used not only to analyze existing data but also to guide sampling, and we expect fully realizing the latter will require systematically comparing existing approaches and developing new ones.

We focused on molecular examples, but the underlying framework is general. Indeed, the methods we discussed are already used to study transitions in atmosphere and ocean data [276, 277, 278, 279, 280, 281, 282]. Beyond reinforcement learning, developments in machine learning more broadly, from equivariant graph architectures to generative models, are already shaping analyses of dynamics, and continued exchange in both directions can sharpen sampling strategies, model design, and the theoretical guarantees that accompany them. Much of the progress in computing kinetic statistics made to date reflects a dialog among chemists, physicists, statisticians, applied mathematicians, and computer scientists. We hope this review lowers the barriers that separate these communities and helps researchers apply the methods described here to diverse new systems.
